title: Questions Worth Asking
subtitle: A five-session study for skeptics and seekers asking, honestly, whether Christianity is true.
summary:
This study is for the person who does not believe, or is not sure, and is willing to look anyway. It is also for the friend who invited them, and who is about to learn how much harder it is to defend the faith than to assume it. The man who wrote it spent years as an atheist. He did not pray his way back. He read and argued and resisted his way back, slowly, over objections he still respects, and he has not forgotten what the other side of the door feels like. So nothing here is a trick. There is no emotional ambush waiting in session five, no moment where the lights dim and the music swells and you are asked to decide something you did not come to decide. Each session takes one hard question, states the strongest case against Christianity first and in full, and only then offers the response, and the response is allowed to be incomplete, because honest answers usually are.

This is not a study that wins arguments. It will not turn anyone into a debater, and the leader must not try. It walks through five questions in order. Whether there is anyone there at all. Whether science has buried God. Who Jesus actually was. Whether the resurrection happened. And what kind of step faith finally is, if the evidence does not force it. Along the way it names real thinkers by name, Lewis and Plantinga and Craig and Wright and Bauckham and Habermas, not as authorities to end the conversation but as people who have done the hard work and are worth reading. It is built to be run by a host who is not an expert, who may not know the answers and should say so when that is true. Every question carries the thinking behind it. Every objection is stated at full strength before it is answered. And no question, ever, is met with shame. A person who asks the hard thing out loud is doing the brave and honest thing, and the room exists to make that safe.
audience: Skeptics, seekers, agnostics, and the friends who invited them

sessions.title: Is There Anyone There
sessions.aim: To ask whether the universe is finally personal or finally empty, taking the case for atheism at its full weight, and to put the strongest arguments for God, from fine-tuning and from morality, on the table without overclaiming what they prove.
sessions.summary: Before any question about Jesus or the Bible, there is a prior one that everything else rests on. Is there anyone there. Is the universe, at bottom, a person or a process, a someone or a vast indifferent machine. The skeptic begins with a strong position and it deserves to be stated strongly. The honest default of a scientific age is that there is no one there, that the cosmos is matter and energy unspooling by fixed laws toward heat death, and that the human longing for a someone behind it is exactly the wishful thinking we would expect from a frightened animal that knows it will die. Bell grants the full force of that, because he held it. Then he turns to the two arguments that pulled at him hardest as an unbeliever, and he is careful not to oversell them. The first is fine-tuning, the strange fact that the basic constants of physics sit within ranges so narrow that a tiny change in any direction yields a dead universe, no stars, no chemistry, no anyone to notice. This does not prove God. It does present a fact that demands an explanation, and the explanations on offer, brute luck, a multiverse no one can observe, or a mind behind it, are all in some sense beyond proof. The second is the moral argument, the stubborn human conviction that cruelty is actually wrong, not merely disliked, and the difficulty of grounding that conviction in a universe that is only atoms. If there is no one there, where does the ought come from. Bell does not claim either argument forces belief. He claims they make the personal universe a live and serious option, not the embarrassing relic the age assumes, and that the question is worth asking with the mind fully on.

keyScripture.why: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky proclaims the work of his hands, an ancient claim that the order and grandeur of the physical world is itself a kind of speech, a witness pointing beyond itself, which is precisely the intuition the fine-tuning question revives in modern dress.

discussion.q: Before tonight, when you imagined the universe at its deepest level, did you picture a someone or a something, and where do you think that picture came from?
discussion.behind: Surface the default before arguing anything. Most people carry an unexamined assumption about whether reality is personal, and they have rarely traced where it came from, whether reasoning or upbringing or simply the mood of the age. The aim is not to settle it but to expose the assumption and the fact that it is an assumption. Land it on honesty, not agreement. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: The fine-tuning fact is that the constants of physics sit in extremely narrow ranges that allow a universe with anyone in it. What is your honest first reaction to that, and does it move you at all?
discussion.behind: Get the gut response before the analysis. Some will reach immediately for the multiverse, some will feel a pull they distrust. The point is not to force the inference but to let people feel the genuine strangeness of the fact and notice how quickly they want to explain it away in either direction.

discussion.q: Bell says the moral argument is what nagged him hardest as an atheist, the sense that cruelty is actually wrong and not just disliked. When you call something truly evil, what do you think you are claiming?
discussion.behind: This is the live wire of the session. Press gently on whether moral judgments are reports about reality or only expressions of preference. Do not let it become a debate about whether atheists can be good people, they obviously can. Keep it on the harder question of what grounds the ought. Most people live as moral realists and reason as relativists, and the gap is worth feeling.

discussion.q: Bell refuses to say these arguments prove God. He says they make a personal universe a serious option. Is that too modest, or is the modesty part of what makes it worth hearing?
discussion.behind: Protect the honesty of the method. Some in the room will have been burned by apologetics that claimed to prove too much. The aim is to let them see that an argument can be worth taking seriously without being a knockout, and that overclaiming is its own kind of dishonesty the study refuses.

discussion.q: Bell admits he wanted there to be no one there, because a someone would have a claim on him. Where do you notice your own wants pulling on what you find easy or hard to believe here?
discussion.behind: Move from argument to self-implication, and make clear it cuts both ways, including for the believers in the room who may want God to exist for reasons of comfort. The aim is not to accuse anyone of bad faith but to get everyone honest that desire shapes belief on both sides, which is the beginning of thinking clearly. Go first.

objections.objection: Fine-tuning is no evidence at all. If the constants were different we would not be here to notice, so of course we find ourselves in a universe that permits us. And a multiverse, an unimaginable number of universes with every possible set of constants, explains the apparent tuning with no designer required.
objections.response: Take both halves seriously, because each has real force. The observation that we could only find ourselves in a life-permitting universe is true, but it does not by itself explain why any life-permitting universe exists at all. That a winner cannot complain about winning the lottery does not mean the lottery had no setup. The multiverse is a more serious move, and Bell grants it is coherent, but notice what it costs. It posits an immense unobservable reality to avoid a designer, which is itself a vast metaphysical commitment held by faith, not a laboratory result. So the honest situation is this. The fine-tuning is a real fact that demands an explanation, and the three main candidates, raw luck, an unseen multiverse, and a mind, are each in some way beyond direct proof. The point is not that God is proven. It is that the design inference is at least as respectable as its rivals, and the confident dismissal of it is a bluff.

objections.objection: Morality does not need God. It is explained by evolution and social contract. Cooperation helped our ancestors survive, so we evolved moral instincts, and societies built rules on top of them. There is no need to smuggle in a cosmic lawgiver.
objections.response: Grant the science fully, because it is almost certainly part of the true story. Evolution and culture do shape our moral feelings, and a believer has no reason to deny it. But notice the gap the explanation leaves open. To explain why we have the feeling that cruelty is wrong is not the same as explaining whether cruelty is in fact wrong. An account of how a belief arose says nothing about whether the belief is true. If our sense of justice is only a survival trick, then when you call genocide evil you are not describing reality, you are reporting a preference your genes installed, no more true than a taste for sugar. Most people cannot actually live that way. They believe, all the way down, that the torture of a child is really wrong, not merely unfashionable. Bell does not claim this proves God. He claims that if real moral facts exist, facts that hold whether or not anyone agrees, they are very hard to ground in a universe that is only matter, and the personal universe accounts for them more naturally. The question is whether you can keep the conviction once you have removed its foundation.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If it turned out there really is someone there, behind all of it, who knew your name, would that be the best news you ever heard or the most unwelcome, and what does your answer tell you?
sessions.practice: This week, run one honest experiment with your own mind. Pick a moment when you call something truly wrong, in the news, in your own past, anywhere, and stop and ask what you are actually claiming. Are you saying this is wrong the way it is wrong to wear white after a certain date, a custom, or wrong the way two plus two is not five, a fact. Write down which one you really believe when it is something that matters, and notice whether your stated philosophy and your lived conviction match.
sessions.closingPrayer: We will close with a few honest words, and no one here has to agree with them. If you are there, and we are not sure you are, then we are asking, plainly, to be shown what is true and not only what is comfortable. We are aware that we want things, that our wanting bends what we will look at, and we ask for the honesty to follow the evidence even where we would rather it did not go. If the heavens are declaring anything, give us the patience to actually look up. Amen.
reflection: When I picture the universe at its deepest level, do I picture a someone or a something, and have I ever actually examined why?
When I call something truly evil, am I describing reality or reporting a preference, and can I live consistently with the answer I give?
What do I want to be true about whether anyone is there, and how might that want be shaping what I am willing to consider?
sessions.teaching: Before we say a single word about Jesus or the Bible or the church, we have to ask the question underneath all of those, the one everything else stands on. Is there anyone there. Not is religion useful, not is faith comforting, but is the universe, at its absolute bottom, a person or a process. A someone, or a vast and indifferent machine running down toward the dark. Everything else in this study depends on the answer, so we start there, with the mind fully on. And I want to begin by stating the skeptic's position at its full strength, because it was mine, and I will not caricature a view I held with my whole chest. The honest default of an educated, scientific age is that there is no one there. The cosmos is matter and energy, governed by fixed laws, unspooling from a hot beginning toward a cold end, and it was not made for us and does not know we exist. The human craving for a someone behind it all, a Father, a mind, a meaning, is exactly the wishful projection you would predict from a clever, frightened animal that has just become smart enough to know it is going to die. That is not a stupid position. It is a serious one, held by serious people, and if you hold it, you are in good company and you are welcome in this room exactly as you are. Now let me tell you what pulled at me, as an atheist, against that position. Two things, and I am going to be careful with both, because the fastest way to lose a thinking person is to claim more than you can deliver. The first is what physicists call fine-tuning. Over the last century we have learned that the basic constants of nature, the strength of gravity, the force that binds atomic nuclei, the energy woven into empty space, sit within astonishingly narrow ranges. Move several of them a hair in either direction and you do not get a different universe with different life. You get no universe with anyone in it at all, no stars, no chemistry, no observers, nothing. Now, this does not prove God, and anyone who tells you it does is selling something. There are real responses. Maybe we should not be surprised, since we could only ever find ourselves in a universe that permits us. Maybe there are countless other universes with every possible setting, and we simply inhabit one of the rare livable ones. Both are coherent. But sit with what they cost. The first does not explain why any livable universe exists, only why we see one if it does. And the second buys its way out of a designer by positing an immense, unobservable ocean of other universes, which is a staggering act of faith dressed in a lab coat. So here is the honest situation. The fine-tuning is a real fact. It demands an explanation. And every explanation on the table, brute luck, the unseen multiverse, or a mind behind it, runs past the edge of what can be directly proven. The design inference is not the embarrassing relic the age assumes. It is at least as respectable as its rivals. The confident dismissal is a bluff. The second thing that nagged me was harder, and it would not let go. It is the moral argument, and I will put it as plainly as I can. We do not merely dislike cruelty. We believe it is wrong. When we read about a child tortured for someone's pleasure, we do not think that is not to my taste. We think that is evil, and it would be evil even if every person alive approved of it. That conviction is not a preference. It has the texture of a fact, something we discover rather than invent. Now the atheist has a good account of where the feeling came from, evolution wired us for cooperation, culture built rules on the wiring, and a Christian has no reason to deny a word of it. But notice the gap, because everything lives in this gap. To explain how we came to feel that cruelty is wrong is not to establish that cruelty is wrong. The story of a belief's origin is silent about the belief's truth. And if our deepest moral convictions are only survival tricks our genes installed, then when you say genocide is evil you are not describing the world, you are reporting a feeling, no truer than a preference for sweet over sour. Almost no one can actually live that way. We believe, all the way down, in real right and real wrong, facts that hold whether or not anyone agrees. And those facts are very hard to ground in a universe that is only atoms in motion. C. S. Lewis, who came to faith the long and reluctant way, kept returning to this, the strange authority of the ought, the sense that we are answerable to something we did not make. Again, I am not claiming this proves a someone. I am claiming that if real moral facts exist, a personal universe explains them far more naturally than an impersonal one, and that you cannot keep the conviction indefinitely after you have sawn off the branch it sits on. So I will not overclaim, and I will not let you under-claim either. Neither argument forces belief. Together they do something more modest and more important. They make the personal universe a live, serious, intellectually respectable option, not the relic of a credulous past. And I have to tell you the last thing, the honest thing about myself. Part of why I held the no-one-there view so tightly was that I wanted it. A someone behind the universe would have a claim on me, and I did not want a claim on me. The wanting bent what I was willing to look at. If you are honest, you will find the wanting in yourself too, in one direction or the other, and the believers in this room are not exempt, because wanting God to exist for comfort is its own distortion. The beginning of thinking clearly is admitting the pull. So that is the question, and it is the only one we need tonight. Not is it proven. Is anyone there. And is that a question you have actually let yourself ask, with the mind all the way on and the wanting out on the table where you can see it.

scriptureStudy.note: The heavens declare the glory of God, the sky proclaims the work of his hands. The claim is that the physical order is a kind of speech, a witness pointing past itself, which is the ancient form of the intuition fine-tuning revives.

What can be known about God is plain, his eternal power and divine nature perceived in the things that have been made. Paul claims creation is evidence available to anyone, not a private revelation, which is exactly the terrain a skeptic can examine.

Even those without the law show the work of the law written on their hearts, their conscience bearing witness. The text claims a moral knowledge built into human beings, the very thing the moral argument tries to account for.

Paul tells Athenian philosophers that the God who made the world is not far from any of us, and quotes their own poets back to them. Notice he argues on shared ground, from creation and conscience, not from a Bible they did not accept.

The fool says in his heart there is no God. Read carefully, the Hebrew fool is not the unintelligent person but the one who lives as if the question does not matter, which is a posture, not an IQ. The verse indicts indifference, not honest doubt.
He has put eternity into the human heart. The writer names the restless sense that we are made for more than the visible, the ache that fine-tuning and the moral law both press on.

By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible. The claim is that the visible world rests on an invisible cause, which is, stated plainly, the design question.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long argument over what philosophers call natural theology, the attempt to reason toward God from the world rather than from Scripture, because the questions in this session are old and the strongest versions are worth meeting at full strength on both sides. The medieval thinkers, Aquinas chief among them, framed arguments from causation and contingency, asking why there is something rather than nothing and whether a chain of dependent things can hang on nothing at all. The modern fine-tuning discussion is a fresh chapter in that ancient line, now armed with physics the medievals could not have imagined. On the other side, weigh David Hume, whose criticisms of the design argument in the eighteenth century remain the sharpest ever written and which every honest believer should read before claiming the argument is settled. Set the contemporary defenders, William Lane Craig on the cosmological and moral arguments and Alvin Plantinga on whether belief in God can be rational without proof at all, against their serious critics, and notice that the live debate is genuinely live, conducted by capable people on both sides, not closed in either direction. A serious group should resist two temptations, the believer's temptation to treat these arguments as knockdown proofs, which they are not, and the skeptic's temptation to treat them as long-refuted embarrassments, which they also are not. The honest finding is that the existence of a personal God is a reasonable position held by reasonable people, that the arguments raise the probability without compelling assent, and that where the evidence stops, a decision begins, which is precisely the ground the final session walks.
sessions.caseStudy: A graduate student named Marcus comes to the group certain there is no one there, and he says so plainly in the first ten minutes, that the universe is matter and energy and that meaning is something humans paint onto it to feel less alone. The host does not argue. He asks Marcus the fine-tuning question and watches him reach immediately for the multiverse, which is the responsible move, and then asks, gently, whether positing countless unobservable universes to avoid a designer is itself a kind of faith. Marcus pauses, because no one has put it to him that way, and admits it might be. Later, on the moral argument, Marcus says cruelty is wrong because it causes suffering, and the host asks whether suffering is wrong as a matter of fact or only as a matter of his preference, and Marcus, who is honest, says he believes it is really wrong and cannot fully say why on his own view. He leaves no more convinced of God, but he leaves having noticed that his certainty was less examined than he thought, and that is exactly what the session is for. The host did not win. He helped a thinking man see his own assumptions, which is the only kind of progress this study counts.

sessions.title: Hasn't Science Buried God
sessions.aim: To take the supposed war between science and faith at its full strength and then to show it is largely a story we have been told rather than a fact we have found, distinguishing what science actually establishes from the philosophy quietly smuggled in beside it.
sessions.summary: Everyone knows the story. Religion held the world in superstitious darkness, science arrived with evidence and reason, the two went to war, and science won, leaving God as a fading comfort for people who cannot face the cold facts. It is a powerful story, and the skeptic who holds it is not foolish, because parts of it are true. The church did sometimes resist new knowledge, and faith has often been the enemy of inquiry. Bell grants all of it. Then he asks a harder question. Is the war story actually true as history, and does science, properly understood, actually bury God. On the history, the famous war is largely a nineteenth-century invention, a narrative built by a few polemicists and repeated until it felt like common knowledge, while the actual record shows that modern science was born largely among believers who expected an orderly creation because they believed in an orderly Creator. On the substance, the deeper confusion is a category error. Science tells you how the mechanism works. It is constitutionally silent on whether there is a meaning or a maker behind the mechanism, because those questions are not the kind its instruments can reach. To say there is no God because science found no God is like saying there is no author because you searched the novel and found only sentences. Bell takes the strongest form of the objection, that appealing to God is just a god of the gaps who shrinks every time science explains something new, and he grants the danger is real. But the reply is that the Christian claim was never that God is one cause among the natural causes. It is that he is the author of the whole causal order, the reason there is a lawful universe for science to study at all. The war is not between science and God. It is between two philosophies, and only one of them gets to wear the lab coat in public.

keyScripture.why: In him all things were created, and in him all things hold together, a claim that God is not a gap in the natural order but the ground of the whole order, which is exactly the distinction that dissolves the supposed war between science and faith.

discussion.q: Most of us absorbed the idea that science and religion are at war without ever examining it. Where did you first get that story, and was it ever actually argued to you, or just assumed?
discussion.behind: Expose the narrative as a narrative. The war story is usually inherited atmospherically, from school, film, the general air, rather than reasoned through. The aim is to get the room to notice they hold a strong historical claim they have never checked, which opens the door to checking it.

discussion.q: Bell grants the church really has resisted knowledge at times. What examples come to mind for you, and does honestly naming them make the deeper question easier or harder to discuss?
discussion.behind: Build trust by conceding what is true before disputing what is not. Let the room name Galileo or young-earth fights or whatever they carry. The aim is to show the study is not defensive, that it will grant real failures, which earns the right to then question the larger story.

discussion.q: The claim is that science tells you how the mechanism works but is silent on whether there is meaning behind it. Does that distinction feel honest to you, or like a way of protecting faith from evidence?
discussion.behind: This is the central move, and the most likely place for honest pushback. Some will hear it as a dodge that puts God conveniently out of reach of testing. Let them say so. Then help the room see the difference between a claim science cannot reach and a claim science has refuted, which are not the same thing.

discussion.q: Bell admits the god of the gaps is a real danger, the god who shrinks every time science explains something new. Have you seen faith used that way, and why is that a bad argument even for a believer?
discussion.behind: Concede the strongest version of the objection openly. A god invoked only to plug current ignorance does retreat with every discovery. The aim is to separate that bad argument, which believers should also reject, from the different claim that God grounds the whole lawful order rather than filling its gaps.

discussion.q: Many of the founders of modern science were believers who expected an orderly world because they believed in an orderly maker. Does that surprise you, and what does the surprise reveal about the story we were handed?
discussion.behind: Close on the historical reversal with a light touch of self-implication for everyone, including the leader. The point is not to score a point but to notice how much of what we are certain about turns out to be received rather than examined, on every side, which is the posture the whole study asks for.

objections.objection: Science and religion are obviously at war, and science keeps winning. Every time we used to say God did it, lightning, disease, the origin of species, science later found the real natural cause. God is just the name we give to what we cannot yet explain, and that territory shrinks every year.
objections.response: Concede the real part first, because there is a real part. People have invoked God to explain natural events that later got natural explanations, and a faith that lives only in the gaps of current science is doomed to shrink, and deserves to. A believer should reject the god of the gaps as firmly as any atheist does. But the historic Christian claim was never that God is one more cause inside the chain of natural causes, competing with lightning and germs for the same job. The claim is that God is the author of the entire chain, the reason there is a lawful, intelligible universe in which lightning has causes at all. Finding the natural mechanism of lightning no more eliminates God than discovering how an engine works eliminates the engineer. The two operate at different levels. Science describes the mechanism. The God question is about whether the mechanism has an author, and no amount of mechanism-description can answer it, because that is not the kind of question a mechanism can answer.

objections.objection: If God is real, that should be a testable claim, and it is not. You have just defined God as something science can never touch, which is exactly what you would do if you wanted to protect a belief from ever being disproven. An untestable claim is not a serious claim.
objections.response: This is the sharpest version and it deserves a straight answer, not a dodge. First, plenty of things we rightly believe are not testable by the methods of natural science, that other minds exist, that the past was real and not created five minutes ago with false memories, that torturing the innocent is wrong, that the laws of logic hold. Science itself rests on assumptions it cannot test, the reliability of reason and the uniformity of nature, which are believed, not proven. So the demand that every serious claim be scientifically testable fails its own test, because that demand is not itself scientifically testable. Second, the Christian claim is not wholly untestable. It makes historical claims that can be examined, a man who lived, died, and whose tomb was found empty, which the next two sessions take up directly. The God question is not protected from all evidence. It is protected only from a single method that was never designed to address it, and insisting that method is the only road to truth is a philosophy, not a finding.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you found that the war between science and faith was a story you inherited rather than a fact you established, what else that you are sure of might be inherited rather than examined?
sessions.practice: This week, find one claim you have always assumed is settled science against faith, the war itself, the idea that no serious scientist believes, whatever it is for you, and actually look into the history of it for thirty minutes. Read someone competent on each side, not a meme. Write down whether the claim held up as well as you assumed, and notice how it felt to examine something you were certain about.
sessions.closingPrayer: We will close honestly, and you are free to listen as an observer. If you are the author of this orderly world and not merely a gap in our knowledge of it, then we confess how easily we mistake the description of the mechanism for the whole of the truth. Give us the discipline to know what our methods can reach and what they cannot, and the humility to stop calling a philosophy a finding. Where we have been handed a story and called it knowledge, on any side, show us the difference. Amen.
reflection: Where did I get the idea that science and faith are at war, and have I ever actually examined whether the history supports it?
Can I tell the difference between a claim science has refuted and a claim science was never built to reach, and does that change anything for me?
What beliefs do I hold that are not scientifically testable, and do I therefore think they are not serious, or do I quietly make an exception?
sessions.teaching: Everyone in this room knows the story, because we all grew up inside it. Once upon a time, religion held the human race in superstitious darkness, teaching that the earth was the center and the heavens were perfect and disease was a curse. Then science arrived, with telescopes and evidence and the nerve to look, and the two went to war, and science won, battle after battle, until God was left as a fading comfort for the kind of people who cannot quite face the cold and glorious facts. It is a powerful story. It is told in classrooms and films and the general air we breathe, and if you believe it you are not a fool, because parts of it are simply true. The church has, at times, resisted new knowledge. There have been real fights, real censorship, real cruelty done to inquiry in the name of faith, and I am not going to stand here and pretend otherwise. Grant all of it. Now let me ask the harder questions the story discourages you from asking. Is the war story actually true as history. And does science, rightly understood, actually bury God. Start with the history, because this surprises people. The grand narrative of an age-old war between science and religion is, as a matter of historical scholarship, largely a nineteenth-century invention, and we can name the builders. In 1874 John William Draper published History of the Conflict Between Religion and Science, and in 1896 Andrew Dickson White, the first president of Cornell, published A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom. Two polemics, both enormously popular, both arguing that religion had always been the enemy of science, and both so successful that their thesis stopped feeling like a thesis and became the water we swim in. What almost nobody tells you is what the historians did next. David Lindberg spent a career on the science of the middle ages and found the alleged age of darkness full of churchmen doing serious natural philosophy. Ronald Numbers gathered the field in 2009 under the pointed title Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion and took the warfare legends apart one by one. Among historians of science today, believing and unbelieving alike, the Draper and White thesis is not a live position. It is a museum piece. And the record those historians recovered tells a different and stranger tale. Modern science was born, in large part, among believers, and not by accident. The founders, the men who built the scientific method into a going concern, largely expected the natural world to be orderly, lawful, and intelligible, precisely because they believed it was the work of an orderly, lawful, intelligent Creator. The conviction that the universe would make rational sense, that it was worth the trouble of investigating, grew in soil that was thoroughly theological. That does not prove Christianity. It does demolish the simple story that faith and science are natural enemies, because the same people were often doing both, and seeing no contradiction. Now the deeper question, the substance. Does science bury God. And here the trouble is a category error so common it is almost invisible. Science is the study of the mechanism. It asks how, and it answers that question better than anything humans have ever devised. How does the heart pump, how do species change, how did the universe expand from its beginning. These are magnificent achievements and a Christian should celebrate every one of them. But notice what kind of question science is built to answer, and what kind it is not. Science tells you how the mechanism works. It is constitutionally, by its very method, silent on whether there is a meaning or a maker behind the mechanism, because those are not questions its instruments can reach. To say there is no God because science has not found one is like saying there is no author because you read the entire novel and found only sentences, only characters and plot and not a single appearance by the writer inside the story. Of course you did. That is not how authorship works. The author is the reason there is a story at all, present on every page and visible on none of them in the way a character is. Take the objection at its strongest, because it is a good one and I held it. The believer, the skeptic says, just keeps invoking a god of the gaps. Whatever science cannot yet explain, the believer says God did it, and then science explains it, and God shrinks, and this has happened over and over, lightning, disease, the diversity of life, and the pattern is obvious. God is just the name for the not-yet-explained, and his territory contracts every year. And you know what, the skeptic is right about that god. A god who lives only in the gaps of current knowledge is doomed, and deserves to be, and a thinking believer should reject him as firmly as any atheist. But that was never the Christian claim. God was never proposed as one cause among the natural causes, competing with germs for the job of making people sick. The claim is that God is the author of the entire causal order, the reason there is a lawful and intelligible universe in which germs have predictable effects at all. Discovering the mechanism of disease no more eliminates God than understanding the workings of an engine eliminates the engineer who designed it. They are answers to different questions, operating at different levels, and neither one crowds the other out. Then comes the sharpest form of all, and I will not dodge it. If God is real, the skeptic says, that should be testable, and it is not, and you have conveniently defined God as the one thing science can never touch, which is exactly what a person would do who wanted to protect a belief from ever being disproven. Straight answer. Many things we rightly believe are not testable by natural science. That other people have minds and are not clever robots. That the past actually happened and the world was not created five minutes ago complete with false memories. That torturing the innocent for fun is wrong. That the laws of logic hold. None of these can be put in a test tube, and all of them are more certain to us than most scientific results. Worse for the objection, science itself stands on beliefs it cannot test, the reliability of human reason and the uniformity of nature across time and space, which are assumed, not demonstrated. So the rule that only scientifically testable claims are serious destroys itself, because that rule is not scientifically testable. It is a philosophy, and not a very careful one. And here is what matters most. The Christian claim is not finally a claim that floats forever beyond all evidence. It plants itself in history. It says a particular man lived, taught, was executed under a named Roman official, and was found, his followers insisted, alive again with his tomb empty. That is not a claim immune to investigation. It is a claim that invites it, and we will spend the next two sessions doing exactly that. So the war was never between science and God. Science found the mechanism, in breathtaking detail, and the mechanism is gorgeous, and not one inch of it rules out an author. The real war is between two philosophies, one that says the mechanism is all there is and one that says the mechanism has a maker, and only one of those philosophies has learned to walk around in public wearing the lab coat as if the coat belonged to it. It does not. The coat is science. The claim that the mechanism is all there is, that is not science. That is faith, of a different kind, and it should have to argue for itself like any other.

scriptureStudy.note: In him all things were created, and in him all things hold together. The claim is foundational, not gap-filling, God as the ground of the whole order rather than one cause inside it, which is precisely the distinction the god of the gaps objection misses.

In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Read as a claim about authorship and origin, not a scientific mechanism. The text answers who and why, the very questions science is not built to reach, and is silent on the how that science investigates.

Great are the works of the Lord, studied by all who delight in them. The text commends the study of the natural world as an act of delight, the very impulse that drove many founders of science, not as a threat to faith but as an expression of it.

It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, and the glory of kings to search it out. Investigation is dignified, not forbidden, the searching out of a world made to be searched, which is the theological root of the scientific instinct.

Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth. God answers Job not with a syllogism but by parading the order and immensity of creation, an ancient instance of the cosmos itself as testimony, the grandeur that fine-tuning quantifies.

His eternal power and divine nature have been clearly perceived in the things that have been made. The text claims the made world is evidence accessible to reason, which is why a believer welcomes investigation rather than fearing it.

In him we live and move and have our being. The claim is that God is not a being inside the universe to be located by instruments but the one in whom the whole of it subsists, which is why no instrument inside it could ever bury him.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the actual history of the so-called conflict, because the popular story collapses fast under real scholarship and a serious group should see why. The grand war narrative traces largely to two nineteenth-century books, by John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White, whose polemics were enormously influential and, historians now agree, badly distorted the record. Read against them the work of recent historians of science, who document that the relationship between Christianity and the rise of modern science was far more cooperation than combat, that figures like Kepler, Boyle, and Newton understood their work as the study of God's creation, and that even the famous flashpoints, Galileo above all, were tangled in politics, personality, and patronage at least as much as in any clean clash of faith against evidence. Set beside this the philosophical question the history raises, why modern science arose where it did and not in other sophisticated civilizations, and weigh the argument that the doctrine of a rational Creator who made an orderly, contingent world gave investigators reason to expect that the universe would be both lawful and worth examining empirically. A serious group should also press the other direction honestly, asking where Christians have genuinely obstructed inquiry and earned the suspicion, so that the conversation does not become triumphalist. The discipline here is to separate three different things that the war story fuses, the real and sometimes shameful history of particular conflicts, the manufactured myth of an essential and ancient warfare, and the live philosophical question of whether the success of science supports or undercuts belief in God, and to recognize that only the first is settled, the second is false, and the third remains genuinely open.
sessions.caseStudy: A retired engineer named Dana joins the group because her son told her science had made faith obsolete, and she wants to understand what he means. In the discussion she repeats the line she has absorbed, that no serious scientist believes anymore and that the two have always been at war. The host grants, honestly, that the church has sometimes resisted knowledge, and Dana relaxes, because she expected defensiveness and got a concession instead. Then he asks where she first heard the war story, and she realizes she cannot remember it ever being argued to her, only assumed, everywhere, always. A younger member mentions that many founders of modern science were believers who expected an orderly world from an orderly maker, and Dana, who values evidence, says she would want to check that before accepting it, which the host calls exactly the right instinct and encourages her to do. She leaves not with an answer but with a homework she chose herself, to examine a story she had held as settled fact. The point of the session was never to recruit Dana. It was to show her she had been carrying a conclusion she never examined, on a question she cared about.
