sessions.title: Who Was Jesus, Really
sessions.aim: To move from the question of God in general to the particular man of Nazareth, taking seriously the skeptical accounts of who Jesus was, and pressing the old and underestimated problem of what to do with the things he claimed about himself.
sessions.summary: Almost everyone admires Jesus. The skeptic and the believer often agree he was a great moral teacher, a voice for the poor, a figure of rare compassion who has shaped the conscience of the world. That shared admiration is exactly where the trouble starts, because the gentle teacher of popular imagination is not quite the man the earliest sources describe. The first question is who Jesus actually was, and Bell takes the strong skeptical options at full strength. Maybe the real Jesus was a wise rabbi whose later followers inflated him into something he never claimed to be. Maybe the divine claims are legends that accreted over generations, the historical man buried under decades of myth. These are serious positions held by serious scholars, and they deserve a serious hearing. Then Bell presses the difficulty the gentle-teacher view has always had to swallow. The sources we possess, the earliest ones, do not present a modest sage. They present a man who forgave sins that were not committed against him, who claimed authority over the Sabbath and the law, who accepted worship, who said that he and the Father were one, and who was executed precisely for blasphemy, for making himself equal with God. Lewis put the dilemma in its famous sharp form. A man who said the things Jesus said is not left to us as merely a great moral teacher. He has closed that option off himself. He is either a deluded madman, a deliberate liar, or telling the truth, but the one thing the evidence will not easily allow is the comfortable middle, the tame sage who never claimed to be more than wise. The legend escape is real and must be weighed, but it runs hard against how early and how Jewish the highest claims about Jesus already are. The verdict the session leaves open is not which answer to choose. It is that the easy answer, the nice teacher, may be the one option the man himself ruled out.

keyScripture.why: Jesus tells a paralyzed man his sins are forgiven, and the scribes react exactly as careful monotheists should, asking who can forgive sins but God alone, which shows that the highest claim about Jesus is not a late addition but is woven into the earliest layer of the sources and was understood as such at the time.

discussion.q: Before tonight, who was Jesus in your mind, a teacher, a myth, a good man, something else, and how much of that picture came from the actual sources versus from the culture around you?
discussion.behind: Surface the working picture before testing it. Most people hold a Jesus assembled from films, holidays, and general goodwill, rarely from the texts themselves. The aim is to expose the gap between the inherited figure and the documented one, gently, without implying anyone has been foolish.

discussion.q: Many skeptics and believers agree Jesus was a great moral teacher. Bell says the earliest sources make that the hardest position to hold, not the easiest. Why might the nice-teacher view actually be the fragile one?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. The shared admiration feels safe and obvious. The aim is to let the room feel the pressure Lewis named, that a man making the claims the sources record cannot be filed under merely wise, and that the safe answer is doing a lot of quiet work to ignore the texts.

discussion.q: Bell takes the legend theory seriously, that the divine claims grew over generations after the fact. What would have to be true for that to work, and what in the timing of the sources makes it harder than it sounds?
discussion.behind: Steelman the skeptical option, then test it. The legend view requires long, slow development. The difficulty is how early the highest claims appear, within a couple of decades, among monotheistic Jews for whom worshiping a man was unthinkable. Help the room weigh the time available against the size of the alleged invention.

discussion.q: The trilemma says a man claiming what Jesus claimed is either a liar, a lunatic, or telling the truth, but not merely a fine teacher. Where do you feel the force of that, and where do you want to resist it?
discussion.behind: Let the room push on Lewis's argument honestly, including its real weak point, that it assumes Jesus made the claims, which the legend theory disputes. The aim is not to declare the trilemma airtight but to feel its genuine force once the sources are granted, while naming honestly where it can be challenged.

discussion.q: Bell says he spent years admiring Jesus precisely so he would not have to decide about him, keeping him as a teacher to avoid him as a Lord. Where do you keep something at the level of admiration to avoid letting it make a claim on you?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication that reaches everyone. The move of admiring Jesus to avoid reckoning with him is subtle and common, and the leader should own a version of it. The aim is honest recognition that admiration can be a way of keeping distance, not a verdict but an exposure. Go first.

objections.objection: The divine Jesus is a legend. The historical man was a wise teacher or a failed prophet, and over the decades and centuries his followers slowly inflated him into a god, the way legends always grow. The miracle stories and the divine claims are later additions, not what the real Jesus said about himself.
objections.response: This is the serious objection and it has serious defenders, so weigh it carefully rather than waving it off. Legends do grow, and the instinct is sound. But the legend theory needs time, long stretches of it, for a human teacher to become a worshiped god, and the time does not seem to be there. The earliest sources, including creedal material that scholars across the spectrum date to within a few years of the crucifixion, already present Jesus in the highest terms and already report the resurrection. More striking still, the highest claims arise among first-century Jews, fierce monotheists for whom worshiping any human being was the gravest blasphemy imaginable, which is the least likely soil on earth for a man-made-god legend to sprout quickly. N. T. Wright has spent decades on exactly this, how astonishing it is that strict monotheists began worshiping a crucified Galilean within years, not centuries. The legend theory does not vanish, but it has to explain a very large effect in a very short time among the very people least disposed to produce it.

objections.objection: Even if Jesus said those things, claiming to be divine does not make you divine. Plenty of people have claimed to be God or to speak for God. They were deluded or manipulative. Why should Jesus get a different verdict than any other self-proclaimed messiah or guru?
objections.response: Fair, and the trilemma alone does not answer it, because liar and lunatic are live options that must be honestly weighed, not dismissed. So weigh them. The lunatic option has to account for the rest of the portrait, the moral depth, the psychological steadiness under pressure, the teaching that has commanded the respect of friend and foe for two thousand years, which is a strange profile for a man deluded about being God, since such delusions usually come wrapped in obvious instability. The liar option has to explain why a deceiver would invent a message that led him to torture and execution with nothing earthly to gain, and why his closest followers, who knew whether it was a con, went to their own deaths insisting it was true. Neither is impossible, and an honest skeptic can land on one of them. But that is the point of the session. The verdict that takes almost no work, the nice teacher, is the one the evidence makes hardest. Whatever you decide, you are deciding among liar, lunatic, and Lord, and the comfortable fourth option has quietly left the table.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If Jesus really said and meant the things the earliest sources put in his mouth, then admiring him as a great teacher is no longer available to you, so which of the remaining options would you least want to be true, and why that one?
sessions.practice: This week, read the Gospel of Mark straight through, which takes about ninety minutes, the way you would read any short ancient biography, and do one thing as you go. Mark every place where Jesus says or does something that a merely wise teacher would not say or do, claims to forgive sin, accepts worship, speaks with authority over the law. Write down whether the man you actually find on the page matches the gentle teacher of popular imagination, and where he does not.
sessions.closingPrayer: We will close plainly, and you are welcome only to listen. If you were who the earliest witnesses said you were, then we have often kept you at the safe distance of admiration so we would never have to face the harder question. Give us the honesty to read the actual sources rather than the convenient picture, and the courage to let the man on the page be as strange and as demanding as he is, rather than the one we assembled to keep ourselves comfortable. Show us who you really were. Amen.
reflection: How much of my picture of Jesus came from the earliest sources, and how much from films, holidays, and the general culture around me?
If the gentle-teacher view is the hardest one to hold once I read the texts, what work has that view been quietly doing for me?
Among liar, lunatic, and Lord, which would I least want to be true, and is it possible I have avoided choosing precisely to avoid that one?
sessions.teaching: We have asked whether anyone is there, and whether science buried the question, and now we narrow from God in general to one particular man, because Christianity does not finally rest on an argument from physics or philosophy. It rests on a person, a first-century Galilean Jew named Jesus of Nazareth, and the only honest way forward is to ask, with the mind all the way on, who he actually was. And here is the strange thing, the thing that makes this the most interesting question of the five. Almost everyone admires him. The skeptic in this room and the believer beside them very likely agree that Jesus was a remarkable moral teacher, a champion of the poor and the outcast, a figure of rare compassion whose words have shaped the conscience of the whole world. That agreement feels like common ground, and it is, but it is also exactly where the trouble starts, because the gentle teacher we all admire is not quite the man the earliest sources actually describe. So take the skeptical options first, at full strength, because they are serious and held by serious people. The first says the real Jesus was a wise rabbi, a teacher of love and reversal, whose followers later inflated him into something he never claimed to be, draping a divine costume over a human sage. The second says the divine claims are legend, myth that accreted slowly over generations, the historical man long buried under decades of pious storytelling, the miracles and the God-talk added by later hands. These are not foolish positions. They are defended by capable scholars, and if you hold one of them you are not being stupid, you are doing what thoughtful people do, looking for the most ordinary explanation of an extraordinary set of texts. They deserve a real hearing, and I will give the legend theory a serious test in a moment. But first, sit with the difficulty the nice-teacher view has always had to swallow, because it is larger than people expect. The sources we actually possess, the earliest layers, the material closest to the events, do not hand us a modest sage offering tips for living. They hand us a man who did things and said things that, for a first-century Jew, were either true or monstrous, with very little room in between. He forgave sins, and not sins committed against himself, which is the prerogative of the one offended, so that to forgive a stranger's sins against others is to stand in the place of God, and the scribes watching understood this instantly and called it blasphemy. He claimed authority over the Sabbath and over the law of Moses, which no rabbi would dare. He accepted worship rather than refusing it in horror as any pious Jew or angel in the texts always does. He spoke of himself and the Father as one. And he was executed, in the end, not for teaching kindness, which gets no one crucified, but on a charge of blasphemy, for making himself equal with God. This is where C. S. Lewis, who came to all of this as a reluctant convert from atheism, put the matter in the sharp form that has annoyed and gripped people ever since. A man who was merely a man and said the sort of things Jesus said, Lewis argued, is not a great moral teacher. He has himself closed that door. He would be on the level of a man who claims to be a poached egg, a lunatic, or else a liar, or else he is exactly who he said. You can spit at him or you can fall at his feet, but the one thing you are not permitted to do, if you take the sources seriously, is the patronizing thing, calling him a fine human teacher and leaving it there. He has not left that open to us. He did not intend to. Now I promised the legend theory a real test, so here it is, and this is where it gets hard for the skeptic. Legends do grow, that instinct is correct. But legends need time, long stretches of it, for a human teacher to ripen into a worshiped god. And the time does not appear to be there. The earliest sources we have, including creedal formulas embedded in Paul's letters that scholars across the whole spectrum, believing and skeptical, date to within a handful of years of the crucifixion, already proclaim the resurrection and already speak of Jesus in the very highest terms. Worship of him is not a fourth-century development. It is right there at the start. And then the detail that should genuinely give a thoughtful skeptic pause. All of this erupted among first-century Jews, who were not loose polytheists ready to add another god to a crowded shelf, but the fiercest monotheists in the ancient world, for whom worshiping any human being was the unthinkable, damnable sin. That is the least promising soil on the entire planet for a man-made-god legend to grow, and grow fast. N. T. Wright has given much of his career to precisely this puzzle, the sheer historical strangeness that strict monotheists began, within a few years and not a few centuries, worshiping a crucified Galilean as Lord. The legend theory does not simply collapse, and an honest person can keep working at it. But it now has to explain an enormous effect in a tiny window of time among exactly the people least likely to produce it, and that is a much heavier lift than the casual phrase legends grow lets on. So weigh the options honestly, all of them. Maybe he was a lunatic, deluded about his own divinity, except that the rest of the portrait, the moral genius, the unnerving steadiness, the teaching that has held the respect of his enemies for two thousand years, is a strange profile for a man so deceived about himself, since that kind of delusion usually trails obvious wreckage behind it. Maybe he was a liar, except that the lie cost him torture and a brutal death with nothing earthly to gain, and his closest friends, the ones who would have known if it was a con, went to their own deaths refusing to take it back. Neither liar nor lunatic is impossible, and I will not pretend otherwise. An honest skeptic can plant a flag on one of them and I will respect it. But notice what has happened. The verdict that costs you nothing, the one everyone reaches for by reflex, the nice teacher, is the single option the evidence makes hardest to hold. And I have to confess my own version of this, because I lived in it for years. I admired Jesus precisely so that I would not have to decide about him. I kept him filed safely under great teacher, where he could inspire me and ask nothing of me, because a teacher you can applaud and walk away from, but a Lord has a claim on you, and I did not want a claim on me. The admiration was not the beginning of taking him seriously. It was my way of not taking him seriously while looking like I did. So that is the question, and we do not have to answer it tonight. Who was Jesus, really. Read the actual sources, not the picture you inherited. And when you do, you may find that the comfortable middle ground you have been standing on, the gentle sage who never claimed to be more, is the one patch of ground the man himself dug out from under you.

scriptureStudy.note: Jesus tells a paralytic his sins are forgiven, and the scribes ask who can forgive sins but God alone. The reaction is the tell, careful monotheists hearing a divine claim and recognizing it instantly, which places the high claim in the earliest layer, not a late one.

Asked if he is the Christ, Jesus answers in terms the high priest hears as blasphemy, and the council condemns him for it. He is executed not for teaching kindness but for a claim about his own identity, which the nice-teacher view cannot accommodate.

I and the Father are one, and the crowd takes up stones because, they say, you being a man make yourself God. Whatever one concludes, the text shows the claim was understood as a claim to deity by those who heard it, not a later gloss.

Before Abraham was, I am. Jesus uses the divine name of Exodus for himself, and again the response is an attempt to stone him, which only makes sense if the hearers grasped the magnitude of what was claimed.
Who do you say that I am. Jesus presses the identity question directly onto his followers, refusing to let it stay abstract, which is the same question the session refuses to let the room avoid.

An early hymn, likely predating the letter, confessing Jesus as in the form of God and worthy of the name above every name. The exalted view is embedded in material scholars date very early, which weighs against slow legendary growth.

Paul hands on as of first importance a creed about Christ's death and resurrection that scholars across the spectrum date to within a few years of the events, evidence that the highest claims were primitive, not the product of generations.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the scholarly quest for the historical Jesus, because the question who was Jesus really has been pursued for more than two centuries by capable people on every side, and a serious group should know the terrain rather than the slogans. The modern study runs through several phases, from the nineteenth-century attempts that often produced a Jesus suspiciously like the scholars writing them, through the mid-twentieth-century skepticism that doubted how much could be known at all, to the more recent recovery of Jesus firmly within his first-century Jewish world. Read the range honestly. On the skeptical end, weigh the work of those who argue the Gospels are theology rather than history and that the divine Jesus is a development, represented by figures associated with the Jesus Seminar. Against them, read N. T. Wright, whose multivolume study places Jesus convincingly within Second Temple Judaism and argues that his self-understanding and the rise of resurrection belief are best explained by something close to the church's claim, and Richard Bauckham, whose work argues the Gospels rest on named eyewitness testimony rather than anonymous drifting tradition. Weigh too the question of dating and the criteria historians use, multiple attestation, embarrassment, dissimilarity, and where those criteria are strong and where they are contested. The discipline for a serious group is to resist both the popular skeptical confidence that the historical Jesus is unknowable or obviously mythologized and the apologetic temptation to claim the sources are simpler and more harmonized than they are. The honest finding is that the earliest material presents a figure who claimed an authority belonging to God alone, that this claim is early rather than late, and that the question Lewis sharpened, what to do with such a man, is not a trick but the real question the history hands us.
sessions.caseStudy: A man named Tope, raised vaguely religious and now firmly secular, tells the group he admires Jesus enormously, the teaching about the poor, the forgiveness, the courage, and that this is precisely why he resents Christians who turned a good man into a god. The host thanks him and then asks him to do one thing before the next session, to read the Gospel of Mark straight through and mark every place where Jesus says or does something a merely wise teacher would not. Tope comes back unsettled. He had not noticed how often the man forgives sins, accepts worship, claims authority over the law, and he says, with some frustration, that the gentle teacher he admired is harder to find on the page than he assumed. The host does not pounce. He simply names the situation Lewis named, that the nice-teacher verdict is the one the sources make hardest, and asks Tope which of the remaining options he finds least believable and why. Tope is not converted. He is, for the first time, actually reckoning with the man instead of the picture, which is the only thing the session ever set out to do.

memoryVerse.text: He said to them, But who do you say that I am?

sessions.title: Did the Resurrection Happen
sessions.aim: To put the central historical claim of Christianity on the table as a question of evidence, taking the natural explanations at full strength, and weighing the minimal facts that even most skeptical historians grant against the explanations on offer.
sessions.summary: Christianity stakes everything on one event in history, and says so itself. Not a teaching, not a feeling, but a claim about something that did or did not happen in the world, that a crucified man was dead and then was not. Paul wrote that if it did not happen the whole thing is worthless and his readers are fools to be pitied, which is a strange thing for a religion to put in writing unless it means to be tested. So this session treats the resurrection as what it is, a historical question, and works the way a historian works. Bell takes the natural explanations at full strength, because they are the responsible first move. Maybe the disciples stole the body. Maybe they hallucinated their grief into visions. Maybe Jesus never fully died. Maybe the whole thing is later legend. Each deserves a fair hearing. Then he introduces the approach associated with Gary Habermas and others, the minimal facts method, which builds only on data granted by the great majority of scholars who study the period, including skeptical ones. A short list survives that near-consensus. Jesus died by crucifixion. His followers sincerely believed they saw him alive afterward and were transformed by it, some to the point of dying for the claim. The persecutor Paul and the skeptic James were both turned by what they were convinced were appearances. And the proclamation of the resurrection began in Jerusalem, the one city where a body in a tomb could have ended it. The question the session presses is not whether you must believe, but which explanation best accounts for that surviving set of facts. The natural theories each strain against one piece or another. The session does not declare the case closed. It declares the case real, the kind of question an honest mind cannot wave away with a slogan about how dead people stay dead, which is true, and is exactly why the witnesses found it so hard to believe themselves.

keyScripture.why: If Christ has not been raised, Paul writes, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain, the rare case of a faith staking its entire truth on a public historical event and inviting the test, which is why the resurrection can be examined as evidence rather than only believed as doctrine.

discussion.q: Paul wrote that if the resurrection did not happen, the whole faith is worthless and believers are to be pitied. What do you make of a religion that stakes its entire truth on one testable historical claim?
discussion.behind: Open on the strangeness of the wager. Most assume religion is about private feeling immune to facts. The aim is to let the room see that this faith volunteered to be falsifiable, which is unusual, and that the volunteering invites exactly the historical scrutiny the session is about to apply.

discussion.q: Before weighing the evidence, what is your honest prior, how unlikely does a resurrection seem to you on a scale, and does that prior settle the question before any evidence is heard?
discussion.behind: Get the room to notice the role of starting assumptions. Someone certain miracles are impossible has decided the case before opening the file. The aim is not to dislodge the prior but to make people see it is doing work, and to ask whether it is a conclusion from evidence or a commitment held in advance, echoing session two.

discussion.q: The minimal facts approach builds only on data most scholars grant, including skeptical ones, the death, the sincere belief in appearances, Paul and James, the Jerusalem preaching. Which of those facts surprises you most that skeptics concede?
discussion.behind: Establish the shared ground before the explanations. Many assume the skeptic denies everything, when in fact a core is widely granted. The aim is to move the discussion from did anything happen to what best explains the agreed facts, which is the more honest and more interesting question.

discussion.q: Take the natural explanations one at a time, theft, hallucination, a swoon, legend. Which feels strongest to you, and where do you feel it straining against one of the agreed facts?
discussion.behind: Steelman the alternatives and then test them against the data, fairly. Each theory has a real appeal and a real difficulty, theft against the disciples dying for it, hallucination against group and varied appearances, swoon against Roman execution and a sealed tomb. The aim is honest weighing, not a rigged contest. Let people defend the theories.

discussion.q: Bell says that as an atheist he assumed the resurrection was obviously false and had simply never looked, that the certainty came before the inquiry. Where have you been certain about something precisely because you never examined it?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication for the whole room, believers included. The point is the ordinary human move of holding a confident verdict on a question one has never actually studied. The aim is honest recognition, not a push toward belief, that certainty and investigation are different things. Go first.

objections.objection: Dead people stay dead. That is the most reliable fact we have, confirmed countless times every day, and no amount of old testimony can outweigh it. The far more likely explanation is always that the witnesses were mistaken, lying, or legendary, because any of those happens constantly and resurrections never do.
objections.response: This is the strongest objection there is, the one Hume framed, and it must be granted its full weight, because it is largely right. Dead people do stay dead, that is exactly why the resurrection would be a miracle and not a medical footnote, and the witnesses knew it as well as we do, which is why they did not believe it at first either. So the question is not whether resurrection is unusual, it obviously is, but whether the prior improbability is so total that no possible evidence could ever count, and that is a philosophical claim, not a historical finding. If you have decided in advance that the natural world is a closed system no matter what, then you have settled the case before reading a single source, and you should at least be honest that the verdict came before the evidence. If instead the question of whether anyone is there remains open, as the first session argued it reasonably does, then a personal God who made the order could act within it, and the prior is no longer infinite. The evidence cannot be weighed at all until the door is at least left ajar.

objections.objection: The minimal facts are not as solid as you make them sound, and even if they are, the disciples sincerely believing they saw Jesus only proves they had experiences, not that the experiences were real. Grief produces vivid visions of the dead all the time. People see lost loved ones. That is well documented and entirely natural.
objections.response: Grant the real part, because it is real. Grieving people do sometimes have vivid experiences of the dead, this is well attested and no one should deny it, and sincere belief proves sincerity, not accuracy. But weigh how far that explanation actually reaches against the agreed data. Grief visions are private and individual, while the sources report appearances to groups, to many at once, to people who were not grieving and not expecting it, including the skeptic James and the active persecutor Paul, who was not mourning a teacher he loved but hunting a movement he hated. Hallucinations also do not produce an empty tomb, and they do not explain why the authorities in Jerusalem, who had every motive to end the movement by producing the body, apparently could not. The hallucination theory accounts for some of the data well and other parts of it poorly, which is the honest situation with every natural theory here. None is absurd. Each strains against at least one of the facts the scholars grant. The question the session leaves with you is which strain you find easiest to live with, and whether the resurrection itself strains less.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the resurrection actually happened, in history, the way the witnesses said, then everything Jesus claimed about himself was vindicated, so are you more afraid that it is false, or that it is true?
sessions.practice: This week, do what a historian or a juror would do. Read the resurrection accounts in all four Gospels and the early creed in First Corinthians fifteen, side by side, and make two honest lists, the points where the accounts agree and the points where they differ. Then ask the question a careful investigator asks. Do the differences look like the contradictions of invention, or like the ordinary variation of real witnesses describing the same event from different angles. Write down your verdict and your reason.
sessions.closingPrayer: We will close honestly, and you owe these words nothing. If it happened, if you were dead and then were not, then we ask for the rarest thing, the willingness to follow the evidence on a question we would rather keep closed. Strip away the certainty we never earned, the verdict we reached without ever looking, on any side. Where we have been afraid of the answer more than we have wanted the truth, give us courage. And if the tomb was empty, do not let us be the kind of people who refuse to look because of what we would have to do about it. Amen.
reflection: What is my actual prior on whether a resurrection could happen, and is that a conclusion I reasoned to or a commitment I started with?
Of the natural explanations, which do I find strongest, and can I be honest about where it strains against the facts most historians grant?
Am I more afraid that the resurrection is false or that it is true, and what does my answer reveal about what I am really weighing?
sessions.teaching: Christianity is unusual among the religions of the world in this one respect, and it is the respect that matters most tonight. It stakes its entire truth on something that either happened or did not happen in history, a public event in the world, open in principle to investigation, and it says so itself, in writing, from the beginning. Paul put it about as bluntly as a man can. If Christ has not been raised, he wrote, then our preaching is worthless and your faith is worthless, and we are, of all people, the most to be pitied. That is a remarkable thing for the founder of a movement to commit to paper. He did not say the resurrection is a beautiful symbol of renewal that remains true in your heart whatever happened to the body. He said if the body stayed in the tomb, throw the whole thing out and pity us for believing it. A faith that volunteers to be falsified is a faith that is inviting you to check, and so tonight we check, the way a historian checks, with the mind all the way on. Begin where an honest inquiry begins, with the natural explanations, taken at full strength, because reaching for the ordinary before the extraordinary is not skepticism, it is responsibility. Maybe the disciples stole the body and lied. Maybe, crushed by grief, they hallucinated their longing into visions of a living Lord. Maybe Jesus did not fully die on the cross but swooned and later revived. Maybe the whole resurrection account is legend, grown in the retelling over the decades. Each of these is a serious proposal, each has been defended by serious people, and each deserves a fair hearing rather than a quick dismissal, and I will give them one. But before we weigh them, we need to agree on what we are explaining, and here is where the conversation gets more interesting than most people expect. There is an approach to this question associated with the historian Gary Habermas, sometimes called the minimal facts method, and its discipline is severe and worth respecting. It refuses to build on anything that requires you to already trust the Bible as the word of God. It builds only on the data granted by the overwhelming majority of scholars who study this period, including the skeptical ones, the ones with no stake in the resurrection being true. And when you restrict yourself that strictly, a short and stubborn list still survives. First, that Jesus died by Roman crucifixion. This is about as certain as ancient history gets, attested inside and outside the New Testament, and the Romans were efficient at killing. Second, that very soon afterward his followers sincerely believed they had seen him alive, and were so transformed by that belief that some of them died rather than recant it, which proves at minimum that they were not knowingly lying, since people will die for what they wrongly believe to be true but not for what they know to be a hoax. Third, that two men who were not friendly to the movement, the persecutor Paul and Jesus' own skeptical brother James, were each converted by what they were convinced was an appearance of the risen Jesus. And fourth, that the proclamation of the resurrection began in Jerusalem, within weeks, in the very city where the execution had happened and where the tomb was, the one place on earth where producing the corpse would have strangled the movement in its cradle, and yet no corpse was produced. Now hold those four facts, granted by skeptics, and run the natural theories against them, fairly. The theft theory, that the disciples stole the body and lied, runs hard against the second fact, because men do not generally accept torture and execution to protect what they know to be their own fabrication. The hallucination theory has real appeal, since grieving people do sometimes have vivid experiences of the dead, and we should grant that honestly. But it strains against the reports of appearances to groups, to many at once, and against the conversions of James and Paul, who were not grief-stricken mourners primed to see their beloved teacher but, in Paul's case, an active enemy hunting the movement down. And hallucinations, whatever else they do, do not empty tombs or silence authorities who only needed to produce a body. The swoon theory, that Jesus survived the cross, asks you to believe that a man scourged and crucified and speared, sealed in a tomb without medical care, revived on his own, rolled away the stone, overpowered the guard, and then so convinced his followers he had conquered death that they worshiped him, when in truth he would have appeared as a half-dead torture victim desperately in need of a physician. And the legend theory runs into the same wall we hit last session, the shortness of the time and the earliness of the sources, with the resurrection proclaimed in creedal form within a few years among people who could still remember. I want to be careful and fair here, because this is exactly the place where apologetics overreaches and a thinking person rightly recoils. I am not telling you the case is closed and only a fool resists. Each of these natural theories is a real attempt by serious people, and each one explains some of the data. What I am telling you is that each one also strains, badly, against at least one of the facts that even the skeptics grant, and that the resurrection itself, strange as it is, has the odd property of accounting for all four at once. So the honest question is not whether you are compelled to believe. It is which explanation strains the least, and whether you have actually done the work of asking, or only assumed the answer. And that brings me to the strongest objection of all, the one I held myself, the one David Hume framed centuries ago. Dead people stay dead. It is the most reliable pattern we know, confirmed every single day, and surely no pile of old testimony can outweigh the most certain fact in human experience. And you know what, that is largely right, and it must be granted its full force. Dead people do stay dead. That is precisely why this would be a miracle and not a medical curiosity, and it is precisely why the witnesses themselves did not believe it at first, why the accounts are full of doubt and fear and people refusing to credit the women's report. They knew death as well as we do. So the real question hidden inside the objection is this. Is the improbability of resurrection so absolute that no possible evidence could ever count for it. And notice, that is not a historical finding. It is a philosophical commitment, the very one we examined in session two, the assumption that the natural world is a closed system no matter what. If you have decided that in advance, then you settled this case before you opened a single source, and the only honest thing is to admit the verdict came before the evidence, not from it. But if the question of whether anyone is there is still genuinely open, as I argued in the first session it reasonably is, then a personal God who authored the natural order could act within it, and the prior improbability, while still real, is no longer infinite, and the evidence is finally allowed into the room to be weighed. And I have to tell you the truth about myself, because it is the whole reason I take this seriously. As an atheist, I knew the resurrection was false. I was certain of it. And one day, with some embarrassment, I realized that I had never actually examined the evidence for it, not once. My certainty had come entirely before the inquiry. I had inherited the verdict and called it knowledge, which is exactly the thing I prided myself on never doing. So I will not ask you to believe tonight. I will ask you the smaller and harder thing. Have you looked. Or have you been certain about an empty tomb you never once walked up to and examined.

scriptureStudy.note: The early creed listing the death, burial, resurrection, and appearances, including to more than five hundred at once, many still living. Paul invites verification by naming witnesses who could be questioned, the move of a man making a checkable claim.

If Christ has not been raised, our faith is in vain and we are most to be pitied. Paul stakes everything on the event and refuses any symbolic escape hatch, which is what makes the claim a historical question and not only a devotional one.

The women find the tomb empty and flee in fear. The earliest account ends not in triumph but in terror and silence, an awkward, unflattering detail that reads more like memory than like a story designed to convince.

The risen Jesus eats fish and invites them to touch him, the account insisting on a bodily resurrection and not a ghost or a vision, which is the specific claim the hallucination theory must explain away.

Thomas refuses to believe without physical evidence and is not rebuked for wanting it, only invited to examine it. The text portrays doubt being met with evidence rather than with shame, which is the posture of this whole session.

Peter preaches the resurrection in Jerusalem within weeks, to people who witnessed the events, in the very city where the body lay. The boldness of the location is itself evidence, since a corpse would have ended the sermon.

The persecutor Saul is stopped and converted by what he is convinced is the risen Christ. The turning of an active enemy, with everything to lose and nothing earthly to gain, is one of the minimal facts the natural theories must account for.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the historical study of the resurrection seriously, because it is one of the most worked-over questions in the field and a serious group should meet the strongest voices on each side rather than a caricature of either. Begin with the philosophical question that governs everything, the one David Hume framed in his essay on miracles, that a wise person proportions belief to evidence and that the uniform experience of death is itself a proof against any report of resurrection. Read Hume directly, then read the careful responses arguing that his argument, taken strictly, would rule out any sufficiently unusual event regardless of evidence, and that it quietly assumes the very closed system it claims to prove. On the historical side, weigh Gary Habermas and Michael Licona, who developed the minimal facts approach and catalogued the scholarly near-consensus on the core data, against the skeptical historians who grant the same facts but prefer natural explanations, and read Bart Ehrman as a careful representative of the view that something happened to the disciples while withholding the supernatural conclusion. Read N. T. Wright's large study, which argues at length that neither the empty tomb alone nor the appearances alone but the two together, set against first-century Jewish beliefs about resurrection, are best explained by an actual resurrection, and weigh the counterarguments fairly. The discipline for a serious group is to keep two questions distinct, the historical question of what the evidence supports and the philosophical question of what is possible in the first place, and to notice that much of what passes for disagreement about the evidence is actually disagreement about the prior, about whether the door to the miraculous is open at all, which is the question the second and first sessions already put on the table and which no amount of historical data can settle by itself.
sessions.caseStudy: A nurse named Priya, who has watched many people die and knows death better than most, says flatly that the resurrection is impossible and that no testimony could ever move her, because dead people stay dead. The host agrees with her completely, which surprises her, and says that is exactly why it would be a miracle and exactly why the witnesses did not believe it at first either. Then he asks the careful question. Is your position that the evidence is weak, or that no evidence could ever count because the natural world is closed. Priya, who is rigorous, recognizes the difference and admits her real view is the second, the closed system, held before any source is read. The host lets that sit without attacking it, only noting that it is a philosophical commitment and not a finding from the evidence. Over the session Priya weighs the natural explanations against the facts most scholars grant and concedes that each strains somewhere, while still holding her prior. She leaves with her unbelief intact but newly honest about where it actually comes from, which the host treats as a genuine and respectable result, because it is.
